title: Stable reversion of carcinoma cells to non-malignant tissue identity

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a controllable treatment that converts established carcinoma cells into cells with a stable, differentiated, non-malignant tissue identity. The converted cells would lose invasive and tumor-forming behavior and maintain that functional correction after treatment ends. Success would require showing that cells from the malignant lineage actually underwent conversion; a tumor replaced by normal cells after cancer-cell killing would not establish this capability. This is a proposed therapeutic target, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

Differentiation therapy provides a clinical precedent for changing cancer-cell behavior by restoring a maturation program. Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) demonstrates the therapeutic importance of that approach, but its successful treatment does not establish stable conversion of carcinomas into normal tissue. The APL review also describes elimination of leukemia-initiating cells, making it an incomplete analogy for a treatment whose defining result would be the durable persistence of functionally corrected carcinoma-derived cells.

An epigenomic reset or another form of cellular reprogramming could be a route to this outcome. Neither a one-time intervention nor any particular molecular mechanism defines the concept. The defining requirement is durable functional correction: differentiated appearance, altered gene expression or changed histone marks alone would not establish a non-malignant tissue identity. Retained cancer-associated mutations would warrant careful testing, but their presence alone would not invalidate a stable functional correction.

significance.text: If demonstrated in patients across unrelated invasive carcinomas, durable reversion would establish a major therapeutic capability: controlling malignancy through cell identity. Its direct consequence would be loss of invasive and tumor-forming behavior in the converted cells. As a conditional assessment, that would substantially expand the ways established cancer can be treated, without requiring the claim that all existing systemic therapies work exclusively through cell killing.

The clinical motivation is substantial. The 20 October 2020 APL review reports complete-remission rates exceeding 90% and overall survival of 85–99% across the ATRA/ATO studies it summarizes. These figures concern all-trans retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide treatment across differing regimens and follow-up periods; they are not a single uniform chemotherapy-free cure rate. The review describes chemotherapy-free treatment for non-high-risk APL, while also attributing a curative contribution to eradication of APL-initiating cells. The precedent therefore supports differentiation as a powerful therapeutic component, rather than proving cure solely by stable state correction.

Loss of malignant behavior would not automatically make a physical tumor mass disappear. Converted cells could remain as tissue, and mass regression, appropriate tissue remodeling and restoration of organ function would each need separate demonstration. A one-time epigenomic intervention, broad applicability across organs and reduced need for continued treatment are possible downstream benefits, not necessary consequences or established properties of the concept.

Durability is central to the potential benefit. The 3 August 2023 Nature Cancer review abstract describes cancer-cell transitions between states involved in initiation, progression, metastasis and treatment resistance, including drug tolerance. That plasticity supplies a reason to test whether an induced non-malignant identity withstands later challenges. Renewed malignant behavior would fail the stability requirement, even if the initial differentiation response appeared convincing.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability to establish is a controllable transition from established malignant epithelial identity to a durable, differentiated, non-invasive and non-tumor-forming state, with demonstrated breadth beyond one carcinoma type. The supplied evidence does not determine which carcinoma genotypes or tissue contexts permit this transition, or whether one intervention could work across them. It also does not substantiate the original broad genetic comparison between most carcinomas and APL, so that comparison cannot establish the scale of the engineering problem.

A central biological barrier is stabilizing the new identity despite cancer-cell plasticity. The Nature Cancer abstract identifies intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms of plasticity associated with growth, metastasis and drug tolerance. This supports investigating whether both the converted cells and their surrounding conditions sustain correction. Because only the abstract and subscription preview were available to the supplied review, it does not establish a specific mechanism that would lock carcinoma cells into a non-malignant state.

Proposed engineering barriers include selecting a suitable differentiated identity, controlling the intervention without disrupting necessary normal tissue behavior, reaching the malignant populations that matter clinically, and preventing unconverted cells from sustaining disease. Another barrier is causal measurement: experiments must distinguish conversion of malignant cells from selective killing, temporary growth arrest or expansion of pre-existing normal cells. These are requirements inferred from the proposed capability, not solutions demonstrated in the supplied sources.

Functional validation is harder than documenting a molecular response. A change in differentiation markers or chromatin state would need to be connected to durable loss of invasive and tumor-forming behavior. If driver mutations remain, the unresolved question is whether their malignant effects are durably constrained, rather than whether the genome has become identical to that of normal tissue. No finite experiment could establish that reversion is permanent under every possible future condition.

current_state.text: The strongest demonstrated clinical achievement in the supplied material is differentiation-based treatment of APL. The fully retained 2020 Frontiers in Oncology review reports complete remission above 90% and overall survival of 85–99% across cited ATRA/ATO studies, with heterogeneous regimens and follow-up. It describes ATRA plus ATO without chemotherapy as recommended therapy for non-high-risk APL at that time. These are dated clinical findings summarized by a review, not evidence that established carcinomas have been durably converted into normal tissue.

The APL mechanism requires a qualification that changes the interpretation of the precedent. The same review describes arsenic trioxide as capable of eradicating APL-initiating cells and links that effect to cure. Consequently, the clinical success cannot be attributed solely to differentiated malignant cells persisting indefinitely in a corrected state. It establishes successful differentiation-based therapy with an additional initiating-cell eradication component.

The 2023 Nature Cancer review abstract supports the relevance of cell-state plasticity across tumor initiation, progression, metastasis and resistance to therapy. Access in the supplied review was limited to a subscription preview and abstract; the article body and figures were unavailable. Although the source index reports an untruncated extraction, that does not establish full-text access. Reference titles and figure listings therefore cannot supply additional verified results about carcinoma reversion or its mechanisms.

The research notes cite a 2023 Biochemical Pharmacology review for the propositions that differentiation alone is insufficient to cure non-APL acute myeloid leukemia, that most recipients of differentiating agents are refractory or relapse, and that mature leukemia-derived cells can dedifferentiate. No article text or retained artifact was supplied for that citation, so the validated review could not check its identity, wording, frequency claim or mechanistic explanation. These propositions remain unverified within this record; the access limitation does not establish that they are false.

The supplied materials establish neither a patient trial demonstrating durable carcinoma-to-non-malignant conversion nor a sufficiently documented search to conclude that no such trial exists as of 1 November 2026. The supplied search and freshness records are empty. The original assertion about hematologic epigenetic drugs likewise lacks supporting text here. The evidence therefore supports a dated APL precedent and a plasticity rationale, while leaving the present-day status of the proposed carcinoma capability unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: in patients with at least two unrelated invasive carcinoma types, treatment causes lineage-verified malignant cells to acquire a differentiated, non-invasive identity, accompanied by tumor regression and functional evidence of lost tumor-forming capacity that persists after treatment withdrawal. Two unrelated types is a proposed threshold for demonstrating breadth beyond one disease, not an established standard or proof of universality.
completion_criteria.label: Durable non-malignant conversion demonstrated clinically across two unrelated carcinoma types

completion_criteria.text: The evidence should establish conversion causally. A proposed evaluation would combine lineage evidence, tissue characterization and functional assays to distinguish corrected carcinoma-derived cells from normal-cell replacement after killing. Differentiated morphology, reduced invasiveness or altered histone marks alone would be insufficient. Tumor regression should be measured separately, because neither loss of malignant behavior nor a molecular state change establishes disappearance of the mass.
completion_criteria.label: Causal evidence distinguishes carcinoma-cell conversion from normal-cell replacement

completion_criteria.text: Durability testing should prespecify treatment-free follow-up, sampling coverage, assay sensitivity and the conditions under which recurrence or tumor-forming activity will be assessed. Negative biopsies would establish no detected malignancy within their sampling limits, rather than permanent absence of tumor-forming capacity. The plasticity described in the supplied Nature Cancer abstract motivates this testing, but the proposed protocol and thresholds are not prescribed by that source.
completion_criteria.label: Prespecified treatment-free follow-up defines recurrence testing and detection limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries include independent confirmation, repeatable results across patients and relevant carcinoma contexts, and explicit reporting of which cells or lesions escape conversion. Evaluation should also address intervention toxicity, effects on normal tissues, persistence and function of converted tissue, and feasibility of reaching the disease sites being treated. Retained driver mutations would be compatible with success only if durable functional correction were demonstrated within the tested conditions. Replication and finite follow-up would establish demonstrated breadth and duration, not literal universality or lifelong certainty.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication confirms conversion with reported escape and practical limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ONC-02, “Sterilizing immune clearance of established metastatic carcinomas,” and ONC-05, “Therapies that drive the whole clonal population to extinction,” share the aim of durable control of established cancer. Their defining outcomes involve clearance or extinction of malignant cells. ONC-06 instead requires evidence that cells from the malignant lineage survive in a durably corrected state. Killing-based and conversion-based treatments could be combined, but clearance alone would not demonstrate reversion.

Roster-based synthesis: ONC-03, “Eradication of dormant disseminated tumor cells that cause late relapse,” overlaps with the need to prevent recurrence from residual disease. ONC-06 would need to establish whether dormant or disseminated populations are converted, unaffected or otherwise controlled; successful correction in a sampled primary tumor would not answer that question. ONC-07, “Body-wide delivery that alters essentially every malignant cell,” concerns treatment reach. Such delivery could enable reversion throughout disease sites, but delivery by itself would not establish a stable non-malignant identity.

Roster-based synthesis: ONC-04, “A shared malignant dependency that renewing normal tissues can spare,” concerns a broadly useful therapeutic vulnerability and selectivity for cancer over renewing normal tissue. A dependency might provide an intervention point for reversion, but identifying one would not demonstrate durable identity correction. Conversely, reversion could require different interventions in different carcinoma contexts and still establish useful breadth.

Roster-based synthesis: ONC-01, “Mortality-reducing detection of lethal cancers while they are still localized,” and ONC-10, “A reliable distinction between early neoplasms that will kill and those that will not,” concern finding and interpreting early disease. ONC-08, “Interception of non-viral precancers before they invade,” and ONC-09, “Prophylactic immunity that prevents the common non-viral cancers,” concern preventing invasive disease. These capabilities could change who needs treatment, while ONC-06 specifically targets conversion of cells in established carcinomas. Reversion of a precancer alone would not establish that capability.

Roster-based synthesis: ONC-11, “Real-time, cell-resolution guidance that makes incomplete cancer surgery uncommon,” concerns more complete physical removal during surgery. ONC-12, “Off-the-shelf cell therapy that matches autologous cures and can be given at ordinary scale,” concerns therapeutic performance and scalable availability of cell therapy. Either might complement carcinoma reversion, but neither establishes it unless malignant-lineage cells are shown to acquire and retain the required corrected identity.

Conceptual synthesis: differentiation therapy, epigenetic regulation and cellular reprogramming overlap with ONC-06 as possible means of changing cell identity. Cancer plasticity supplies both the rationale for attempting such changes and the concern that they may reverse. A one-time epigenomic reset remains a possible implementation within ONC-06, rather than a separate achievement or an established mechanism.

change_log.change: Preserved ONC-06 and its title while defining success through durable functional conversion of malignant-lineage cells.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent despite limitations in individual supporting assertions; lineage and functional requirements distinguish reversion from appearance changes or normal-cell replacement.

change_log.change: Recast APL as a clinical precedent for differentiation-based therapy rather than an achieved example of cure solely through stable state reversion.
change_log.reason: The retained review also attributes a curative contribution to eradication of APL-initiating cells.

change_log.change: Preserved complete-remission rates above 90% and overall survival of 85–99%, with the 2020 date, study heterogeneity and non-high-risk chemotherapy-free scope.
change_log.reason: The numerical range is supported, but it does not describe a single uniform cohort, cure rate or mechanism.

change_log.change: Separated loss of malignant behavior from mass regression, tissue remodeling and organ-function restoration.
change_log.reason: Stable converted cells could remain as tissue; physical disappearance and functional restoration require separate evidence.

change_log.change: Removed the universal characterization of systemic therapy as cell killing and qualified the proposed one-time epigenomic route.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not support that characterization or establish a particular reversion mechanism.

change_log.change: Replaced broad assertions about carcinoma lesion prevalence and the genetic comparison with APL with explicit open questions about feasibility across contexts.
change_log.reason: The supplied review did not substantiate those assertions.

change_log.change: Changed retained driver mutations from an automatic failure condition to a reason for durability testing.
change_log.reason: Persistent mutations alone do not establish malignant behavior; renewed malignancy would violate the proposed criterion.

change_log.change: Retained the non-APL AML citation as an evidence limitation without repeating its quotation or frequency and mechanism claims as established findings.
change_log.reason: No retained source text was available to check them, and missing evidence does not show they are false.

change_log.change: Replaced the asserted absence of a carcinoma trial with a limit on what the supplied materials establish.
change_log.reason: Empty search and freshness records cannot establish the worldwide state of research on 1 November 2026.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion criteria to include lineage verification, functional testing, withdrawal follow-up, assay limits, replication and practical boundaries.
change_log.reason: These additions make conversion and stability assessable while avoiding claims of permanent absence or universality from finite tests.

change_log.change: Preserved the Nature source's subscription-preview limitation despite the source index's untruncated extraction metadata.
change_log.reason: Extraction length does not establish access to the article body or figures.

change_log.change: Added explicit distinctions from every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: Related delivery, prevention, detection, clearance and treatment capabilities should remain distinct from durable carcinoma-cell reversion.

unresolved_issues: Whether any patient trial has demonstrated durable carcinoma-to-non-malignant conversion as of 1 November 2026 remains unresolved because the supplied search and freshness records are empty.
The identity, wording and supporting evidence of the cited 2023 non-APL AML review cannot be checked from the supplied materials.
The Nature Cancer article's full body and figures were unavailable to the supplied review; additional mechanisms or carcinoma-specific findings cannot be inferred from its reference titles.
Which carcinoma genotypes and tissue contexts permit stable correction, and whether a common intervention could work across them, remain open questions.
The necessary treatment-free follow-up, sampling coverage and functional assay sensitivity have not been specified; the proposed criteria are not established standards.
Whether converted cells could support appropriate tissue function, whether masses would regress, and whether residual or disseminated disease could escape remain unresolved.
The supplied materials do not substantiate the original claims about carcinoma lesion prevalence, the genetic contrast with APL or currently used hematologic epigenetic drugs.

brief.title: Lasting conversion of cancer cells into harmless tissue
possible: People with carcinomas, cancers of tissue linings, could receive treatment that turns their cancer cells into mature cells with a stable, non-cancerous identity. Those cells would stop invading nearby tissue or forming tumors, and stay that way after treatment ends.
why: This would give patients another way to control established cancer: changing how malignant cells behave. A lasting change in cell identity would expand what cancer treatment can achieve.

sources.showed: Their review reports successful treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia, a blood cancer, using drugs that help cancer cells mature and eliminate cells that initiate the disease.
sources.quote: Later, ATO was found to be capable of eradicating APL-initiating cells, resulting in a curative effect
sources.cited_for: Helping cancer cells mature can contribute to successful treatment.
sources.not_established: The treatment does not establish lasting survival of corrected carcinoma cells.

sources.who: Andrea Pérez-González, Kevin Bévant and Cédric Blanpain
sources.showed: Their review describes how cancer cells change identity in ways that support tumor growth, spread and resistance to treatment.
sources.cited_for: Cancer cells can change state, making the stability of any corrected identity a central question.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate a treatment that locks carcinoma cells into a lasting non-cancerous identity.

sources.showed: This is a review of the limits of treatments that make cells mature in other forms of acute myeloid leukemia, a blood cancer.
sources.cited_for: It concerns whether maturation alone can sustain control of leukemia.
sources.not_established: It does not establish durable conversion of carcinoma cells into non-cancerous tissue.

shown: The clearest clinical precedent is treatment that helps cells mature in acute promyelocytic leukemia. Xu and Huang report complete remission above 90% across studies. But treatment also eliminates cells that initiate leukemia, so its success cannot be attributed solely to cancer cells remaining in a corrected state.
missing: A treatment would have to convert established carcinoma cells into mature cells that remain non-invasive and unable to form tumors after treatment ends.
Cell tracking would have to prove that the corrected cells came from the cancer, rather than from normal cells replacing killed cancer cells.
Clinical results would have to establish breadth across unrelated carcinomas and show tumor shrinkage.
Independent studies would have to establish safety, converted tissue function and which cells escape treatment.

milestones.label: Lasting clinical conversion across unrelated carcinomas
milestones.explanation: Patients with two unrelated carcinoma types would have to show tracked cancer-cell conversion, tumor shrinkage and lasting loss of tumor-forming ability after treatment ends. This would establish breadth beyond a single disease.

milestones.label: Proof that cancer cells themselves changed
milestones.explanation: Cell tracking, tissue examination and tests of cell behavior would have to distinguish conversion from normal cells replacing killed cancer cells. This would establish what caused the improvement.

milestones.label: Defined follow-up without treatment
milestones.explanation: Follow-up would have to define its duration, sampling, detection limits and tests for returning cancer before treatment ends. This would make claims of lasting correction interpretable.

milestones.label: Independent confirmation with practical limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to repeat conversion and report escaping disease, toxicity, normal-tissue effects, converted tissue function and treatment reach. This would establish reliability and practical boundaries.

uncertain: Which cancer mutations and tissue conditions allow lasting correction, and whether a common treatment could work across them, remain open questions.
The necessary follow-up duration and test sensitivity remain undefined; finite testing cannot establish lifelong stability.
Whether converted tissue would function appropriately, tumor masses would shrink and disease elsewhere would escape remains unresolved.

page.title: Stable phenotypic reversion of carcinoma cells
page.definition: A treatment converts living carcinoma cells, malignant cells of epithelial tissues such as organ linings, into cells with a specialised identity and function. The new identity can belong to a different tissue, as when breast cancer cells become functioning fat cells in experimental models. Stable reversion requires evidence that the converted cells descend from the carcinoma and remain unable to invade tissue or form tumours after treatment ends.

goal.need: Colorectal cancer alone caused an estimated 918,000 deaths worldwide in 2024. In advanced cancers, mutations can restore growth signals even while patients take drugs that block them. For patients whose carcinoma resists treatment, converting invasive cells could keep those cells from seeding new tumours after therapy ends. The benefit would depend on reaching the cells that drive spread. Other cells in the same tumour can resist conversion and continue to grow.

figures.caption: Estimated deaths worldwide in 2024 at two carcinoma sites
figures.note: These are site-based estimates, not counts of patients eligible for reversion therapy.

completion.title: A human study demonstrates carcinoma-cell reversion that persists after treatment ends.
completion.criterion: A prospective human study shows that treatment leaves living, lineage-verified carcinoma-derived cells with a differentiated identity, a function of that cell type, and loss of invasive and tumour-forming behaviour. These properties persist after treatment ends throughout the study's prespecified observation period, within its sampling and assay limits. Clonal evidence distinguishes conversion from cancer-cell killing followed by normal-cell replacement. Success applies to the carcinoma and follow-up interval tested.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no adopted external completion test was located.
completion.basis: The observation period is prespecified for each study. No adopted external duration for stable human carcinoma reversion was identified. In a liver cancer model, clonally related cells regained malignant features when the suppressed cancer-driving gene was reactivated. In a human differentiation-therapy study, liver biopsies showed necrosis and tissue repair. Neither observation establishes persistent conversion of surviving carcinoma cells in patients.

milestones.title: Living carcinoma-derived cells acquire a differentiated identity and a function of that cell type.
milestones.criterion: Living cells of demonstrated carcinoma origin acquire a differentiated identity and perform a measurable function characteristic of that cell type. The functional assay must establish what the cells do beyond showing that they express a differentiation marker.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback grounded in published differentiation experiments; no common external functional-conversion threshold was located.

milestones.title: Converted carcinoma cells in an animal retain non-malignant behaviour after treatment withdrawal.
milestones.criterion: An intervention converts cells within an established carcinoma in an animal into surviving differentiated cells of verified cancer origin. After the intervention ends, those cells retain their differentiated identity and show loss of both invasion and tumour-forming capacity over the reported observation interval.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback informed by the preclinical experiments and published discussion of withdrawal stability; no adopted animal-reversion threshold was located.

milestones.title: Patients with carcinoma receive a reversion candidate at a dose meeting the trial’s toxicity rule.
milestones.criterion: Patients with histologically confirmed carcinoma receive the candidate in a prospectively registered, regulator-authorised first-in-human study. Observed toxicities at a tested dose satisfy that protocol’s rule over its specified observation period. For example, the Australian SON-DP protocol used a 28-day first cycle. If two participants at one dose had a dose-limiting toxicity, the next lower dose qualified as the maximum tolerated dose if at most one of six participants there had such a toxicity.
milestones.set_by: Each candidate’s registered dose-finding protocol. The quoted rule is specific to the Australian SON-DP protocol ACTRN12623000202662, subsequently withdrawn.
milestones.threshold_quote: no more than 1 of the 6 experiences a DLT, then this lower dose level will be considered the MTD.

milestones.title: Treated patients have living carcinoma-derived cells with a non-malignant differentiated identity.
milestones.criterion: During treatment, a prospective clinical study identifies surviving differentiated cells as descendants of the patient’s carcinoma. Those cells perform a function characteristic of their differentiated identity and show loss of invasive and tumour-forming behaviour. The study assesses toxicity in all treated patients.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; EMA describes clinical biomarker validation, but no adopted endpoint establishing human carcinoma-cell reversion was located.

milestones.title: Cells in an established animal carcinoma survive treatment and acquire a differentiated identity.
milestones.criterion: Treatment begins after a carcinoma is established in an animal. Cells identified as descendants of that carcinoma survive in the treated tissue and acquire the characteristics of a specified differentiated cell type. Evidence of cancer origin must distinguish them from normal cells already present or recruited during tissue repair.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback based on in vivo differentiation experiments. No adopted cross-carcinoma test for this stage was identified.

not_found: No registered carcinoma protocol defining lineage-verified conversion and persistence after treatment withdrawal was located.
Full text could not be retrieved for the supplied Nature Cancer and Biochemical Pharmacology reviews.
No regulator, society or programme criterion specifying how long human carcinoma-cell reversion must persist after treatment was identified.
No oncology society or programme statement opposing the pursuit of stable carcinoma-cell reversion was identified.

results.finding: Of three breast carcinoma lines studied, the MDA-MB-231BRMS-GFP chimera showed human milk protein secretion on lactation day 2.
results.detail: The secretion readout was qualitative. The paper does not give the number of chimeras assayed for human alpha-lactalbumin.
results.quote: Human breast cancer cells secrete human milk proteins into the lumen of lactating hosts

results.finding: In chimeras seeded with human breast carcinoma cells, human keratin 8 marked 2 in 5 luminal cells in a count of 100 cells across three outgrowths.
results.quote: Human breast cancer cells integrated in chimeric outgrowths expressed the human mammary luminal marker keratin 8 (hK8)

results.finding: Mouse colorectal tumours contained GFP-relabelled differentiated crypts 14 days after Apc restoration. Sample size for relabelling was unreported.
results.quote:
Re-labeled crypts contained differentiated enterocytes (Krt20 and Villin) and Goblet cells (Muc2) and showed proliferation restricted to the base of the crypt, indicating that even in the presence of a
Kras
mutation, Apc-restored cells can re-establish normal tissue behavior.

results.finding: An invasive mouse colorectal lesion contained GFP-relabelled, Krt20-positive cells after 14 days of Apc restoration. The paper illustrates one lesion.
results.detail: The invasive-lesion image supports carcinoma origin because GFP also labels Cre-recombined cells in normal crypts.
results.quote: In addition to differentiation within the tumor mass, we identified regions of sub-mucosal invasion in Apc-restored animals that showed strong expression of Krt20

results.finding: Eight mice with Kras- or Kras/p53-mutant colorectal tumours had no reported carcinoma relapse for over 15 weeks during Apc restoration.
results.detail: Re-silencing Apc caused regrowth in the separate benign adenoma model. Krt20 staining in a submucosal lesion showed differentiation at an already invaded site.

results.finding: Three colorectal carcinoma cell lines showed increases in 3 enterocyte marker proteins after simultaneous knockdown.
results.quote: Our in vitro results demonstrated that the simultaneous knockdown of the master regulators reverts three colorectal cancer cells into a normal‐like differentiated state resembling enterocytes with reduced proliferation.

results.finding: Xenografts from 3 colorectal carcinoma lines carrying preimplantation knockdown had lower tumour volume and weight (n = 5 measurements, p < 0.001).
LS174T colorectal carcinoma cells acquired differentiation markers and showed reduced nascent protein synthesis after WNT blockade (n = 4, p < 0.0001).
results.detail: Alcian blue staining in treated xenografts showed mucin-associated material. The study did not directly measure secretion by identified converted carcinoma cells.
results.quote: We observed that after prolonged WNT blockade and differentiation (7 days), CRC cell lines and mouse tumoroids exhibited a significant reduction in EU and OP-P incorporation

results.finding: Established PDO7 colorectal xenografts had more KRT20-positive epithelial area after POLR1A-high cell ablation (9 treated, 8 controls, p = 0.0009).
results.detail: Selective killing of POLR1A-high cells can enrich for pre-existing differentiated tumor cells. The endpoint staining did not resolve which surviving cells acquired the phenotype during treatment.
results.quote: It also caused an increase in the number of differentiated cells shown by KRT20 and Alcian blue staining, although this effect was more prominent in PDO7 than in PDO-p18

results.finding: PDO7 colorectal xenografts retained KRT20-positive tumor cells 7 days after withdrawal (n = 6 tumors in the withdrawal growth cohort).
results.detail: The authors attributed late PDO7 regrowth to ablation-resistant cells based on similar regrowth during continuous treatment and resistance in derived organoids. The cells responsible for regrowth were not lineage-traced to their pretreatment state.
results.quote:
Analysis of the remaining tumor mass 7 days after stopping dimerizer treatment showed the presence of KRT20
+
tumor cells in direct contact with the stroma that exhibited largely reduced protein synthesis rates

results.finding: Serum-deprived human PANC-1 cells showed a net 13.7 percentage-point increase in double labeling from intercellular dye transfer across 4 experiments.
results.detail: The net dye-transfer estimate used freshly mixed labeled cells as the baseline for fluorescence spillover.
results.quote: After 48 hours of coincubation of the 2 populations in SFM, a 19.4% ± 5.9% proportion of doubly labeled cells was yielded, that is, a net increase of 13.7% ± 4.6% that could be attributed to dye transfer.

results.finding: SKOV3 ovarian carcinoma cultures deposited calcium and showed increased alkaline phosphatase activity (three experimental repeats, P<0.001).
results.detail: The functional result was measured in vitro during osteogenic induction. The paper reports the number of experimental repeats but gives no numerical effect size for mineral deposition in the text.
results.quote:
Additionally, the activity of ALP, a key indicator of calcification, was also significantly elevated (P<0.001; Figure
1
D).

results.finding: AQP5-transfected MKN45 gastric adenocarcinoma cells showed higher lysate alkaline phosphatase activity than mock controls (n = 6, p < 0.01).
results.detail: The enzyme assay used a synthetic substrate in bulk lysate, so it could not attribute the activity to the cells that acquired the differentiated morphology.
results.quote: Expression of AQP5 significantly increased the activity of alkaline phosphatase

results.finding: Established murine hepatocellular tumour grafts (6 tumours, 5 mice per cohort) yielded differentiated hepatocytes after MYC inactivation, with some persisting up to 8 months.
results.detail: The lineage evidence came from bulk array CGH and was supported by serial transplantation and normal-hepatocyte controls. Tumours regrew when MYC was reactivated.
results.quote:
Even after prolonged MYC inactivation for up to
8 months some of these differentiated tumour cells persisted,
growing under the skin of a SCID mouse (Fig. 3).

results.finding: Established pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma xenografts showed increased mucin staining after 14 days of LGK974 (n = 3 per treatment group).
results.detail: Figure 6D quantified the percentage of blue pixels in tumor sections. That tissue-level measure did not identify the cells producing the mucin.
results.quote: treatment with LGK974-induced cell cycle arrest and differentiation within the xenograft tumors

results.finding: One patient with colorectal adenocarcinoma received RO4929097 at 40 mg on schedule B.
results.detail: The paper gives no first-cycle dose-limiting toxicity count for the 40 mg cohort. CYP3A4 autoinduction halted escalation before a maximum tolerated dose was determined.
results.quote: One patient with colorectal adenocarcinoma with neuroendocrine features achieved a partial response on schedule B at 40 mg and continued treatment for 10 cycles (Appendix Fig A5, online only).

results.finding: First-in-human RXC004 monotherapy included 3 pancreatic cancer patients. At 2 mg, 1 of 6 patients across tumour types had a dose-limiting toxicity.
results.detail: The 2 mg recommendation incorporated safety, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and efficacy. The presentation does not identify the tumour type of the patient with pancreatitis or show that the dose satisfied a prespecified toxicity rule.
results.quote: Dose Limiting Toxicities in 4 pts: Diarrhoea, Colitis and fragility fractures (10mg) Colitis (3mg) Ileitis (3mg) Pancreatitis (2mg)

results.finding: LY900009 phase I trial (35 patients overall, including an ovarian dose-confirmation cohort) recommended 30 mg three times weekly as the maximum tolerated dose.
results.detail: The abstract gives neither the ovarian cohort size nor the tumour type of the patient with dose-limiting mucosal inflammation.
results.quote: The recommended MTD schedule for future studies was 30 mg thrice weekly, which exceeds the target inhibition level observed in preclinical models to promote tumour regression in humans.

definition = "A treatment converts living carcinoma cells, malignant cells of epithelial tissues such as organ linings, into cells with a specialised identity and function. The new identity can belong to a different tissue, as when breast cancer cells become functioning fat cells in experimental models. Stable reversion requires evidence that the converted cells descend from the carcinoma and remain unable to invade tissue or form tumours after treatment ends.". Reason: The breast and liver experiments clarify both the range of cell types a carcinoma cell can become and the distinction between differentiation and lasting loss of malignancy.

goal.need = "Colorectal cancer alone caused an estimated 918,000 deaths worldwide in 2024. In advanced cancers, mutations can restore growth signals even while patients take drugs that block them. For patients whose carcinoma resists treatment, converting invasive cells could keep those cells from seeding new tumours after therapy ends. The benefit would depend on reaching the cells that drive spread. Other cells in the same tumour can resist conversion and continue to grow.". Reason: The leukaemia remission statistic does not explain the burden of carcinoma, the potential benefit of preventing spread, or the limit imposed by cells that resist conversion.

add statement by Qurgen Inc., SON-DP phase I protocol NCT06873659, 2025: "transform cancer cells in situ into normal tissue cells". Reason: The registered SON-DP programme explicitly names conversion into normal tissue cells as its therapeutic aim.

edit completion: basis = "The observation period is prespecified for each study. No adopted external duration for stable human carcinoma reversion was identified. In a liver cancer model, clonally related cells regained malignant features when the suppressed cancer-driving gene was reactivated. In a human differentiation-therapy study, liver biopsies showed necrosis and tissue repair. Neither observation establishes persistent conversion of surviving carcinoma cells in patients."; refs = [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 14, 17]. Reason: The liver studies give concrete reasons to require both lineage evidence and an assessment after withdrawal, even when a tumour regresses or its cells differentiate.
add case "Hepatocellular". Reason: A published first-in-human CD-801 study in nine patients provides indication-specific evidence for hepatocellular carcinoma.
add case "Pancreatic". Reason: The US SON-DP protocol specifies a pancreatic cancer expansion group whose carcinoma results can be assessed separately.
add case "Ovarian". Reason: The US SON-DP protocol specifies an ovarian cancer expansion group whose carcinoma results can be assessed separately.
add case "Gastric". Reason: SON-DP protocol NCT06873659 specifies a gastric cancer expansion group that includes gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma.

edit m1: criterion = "Living cells of demonstrated carcinoma origin acquire a differentiated identity and perform a measurable function characteristic of that cell type. The functional assay must establish what the cells do beyond showing that they express a differentiation marker."; refs = [8, 9, 11, 17]. Reason: The existing criterion mixes the functional test with experiment dates, sample sizes and results.

add milestone after m1: "Cells in an established animal carcinoma survive treatment and acquire a differentiated identity.". Reason: Conversion within an established tumour is an experimental achievement that can be demonstrated before testing whether the converted cells remain non-malignant after withdrawal.

edit m2: criterion = "An intervention converts cells within an established carcinoma in an animal into surviving differentiated cells of verified cancer origin. After the intervention ends, those cells retain their differentiated identity and show loss of both invasion and tumour-forming capacity over the reported observation interval."; refs = [7, 8, 9, 12, 14]. Reason: The animal withdrawal criterion currently includes results obtained during continuing treatment and after modification before implantation.

edit m3: title = "Patients with carcinoma receive a reversion candidate at a dose meeting the trial\u2019s toxicity rule."; criterion = "Patients with histologically confirmed carcinoma receive the candidate in a prospectively registered, regulator-authorised first-in-human study. Observed toxicities at a tested dose satisfy that protocol\u2019s rule over its specified observation period. For example, the Australian SON-DP protocol used a 28-day first cycle. If two participants at one dose had a dose-limiting toxicity, the next lower dose qualified as the maximum tolerated dose if at most one of six participants there had such a toxicity."; set_by = "Each candidate\u2019s registered dose-finding protocol. The quoted rule is specific to the Australian SON-DP protocol ACTRN12623000202662, subsequently withdrawn."; set_by_kind = "protocol"; threshold_quote = "no more than 1 of the 6 experiences a DLT, then this lower dose level will be considered the MTD."; threshold_ref = 18; refs = [10, 15, 17, 18]. Reason: The Australian SON-DP registration supplies a candidate-specific toxicity rule, and the CD-801 publication records a separate human dose-escalation study in hepatocellular carcinoma.

edit m4: criterion = "During treatment, a prospective clinical study identifies surviving differentiated cells as descendants of the patient\u2019s carcinoma. Those cells perform a function characteristic of their differentiated identity and show loss of invasive and tumour-forming behaviour. The study assesses toxicity in all treated patients."; refs = [6, 7, 17]. Reason: The human conversion criterion includes a search verdict where it should specify what observations in treated patients establish conversion.
remove not found 0. Reason: The Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry provides a directly accessible sponsor registration with the SON-DP toxicity rule.

add not found: "No regulator, society or programme criterion specifying how long human carcinoma-cell reversion must persist after treatment was identified.". Reason: The registered dose-finding rules answer a different question from the duration needed to establish stable reversion.

add not found: "No oncology society or programme statement opposing the pursuit of stable carcinoma-cell reversion was identified.". Reason: The question about institutional disagreement has no attributable position statement.
